content: Ritonavir is not typically used as a standalone protease inhibitor (PI) but rather as a pharmacokinetic enhancer to boost the efficacy of other PIs. It is indicated for use in combination with other antiretroviral agents for the treatment of HIV infection. The initial adult dose is 300 mg orally every 12 hours, which can be increased by 100 mg every 12 hours to a maximum of 600 mg every 12 hours over five days, as tolerated. When used as a booster with another PI, the dose ranges from 100 to 400 mg orally daily or divided every 12 hours. Therapy must be carefully monitored in patients with moderate to severe hepatic impairment. For pediatric patients with HIV-1 infection, ritonavir is also used in combination with other antiretroviral agents. It is not used as a sole PI but as a pharmacokinetic enhancer. For children aged ≥1 month, the initial dose is 250 mg/m² orally every 12 hours, increasing by 50 mg/m² every 2–3 days to a target dose of 350–400 mg/m² every 12 hours, not exceeding 600 mg every 12 hours. For adolescents, the dosing is similar to adults, starting at 300 mg orally every 12 hours and increasing by 100 mg every 12 hours to a maximum of 600 mg every 12 hours over five days, as tolerated. Safety and efficacy in children under 1 month of age have not been established. Ritonavir significantly increases the plasma levels or effects of several drugs by inhibiting hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction can lead to severe toxicities or adverse effects, and many co-administrations are contraindicated. Below are specific examples of drug interactions: 1. Alfuzosin: Ritonavir increases alfuzosin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 2. Amiodarone: Ritonavir increases amiodarone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, while amiodarone increases ritonavir levels via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Co-administration is contraindicated. 3. Cobicistat: Ritonavir increases cobicistat levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 4. Conivaptan: Ritonavir increases conivaptan levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 5. Dihydroergotamine (including intranasal): Ritonavir increases dihydroergotamine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 6. Disulfiram: Disulfiram increases ritonavir toxicity by inhibiting aldehyde dehydrogenase. This interaction is specific to ritonavir oral solution, which contains 42% alcohol. Co-administration is contraindicated. 7. Elagolix: Ritonavir increases elagolix levels. Co-administration is contraindicated with strong OATP1B1 inhibitors. 8. Eliglustat: Ritonavir increases eliglustat levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 9. Elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir DF: Ritonavir increases levels of this combination by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 10. Enzalutamide: Ritonavir increases enzalutamide levels, while enzalutamide decreases ritonavir levels. Co-administration is contraindicated. 11. Ergot derivatives (e.g., ergoloid mesylates, ergotamine): Ritonavir increases levels of these drugs by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 12. Finerinone: Ritonavir increases finerinone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 13. Flibanserin: Ritonavir increases flibanserin levels, leading to severe hypotension or syncope. Co-administration is contraindicated. 14. Gepirone: Ritonavir increases gepirone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 15. Irinotecan (including liposomal): Ritonavir increases irinotecan levels via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Co-administration is contraindicated. 16. Ivabradine: Ritonavir increases ivabradine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 17. Lomitapide: Ritonavir increases lomitapide levels several-fold by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 18. Lonafarnib: Ritonavir increases lonafarnib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 19. Lovastatin: Ritonavir increases lovastatin levels, leading to a higher risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Co-administration is contraindicated. 20. Lurasidone: Ritonavir increases lurasidone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 21. Mavacamten: Ritonavir increases mavacamten levels, potentially causing heart failure due to systolic dysfunction. Co-administration is contraindicated. 22. Mavorixafor: Ritonavir increases mavorixafor levels by inhibiting CYP2D6 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 23. Methylergonovine: Ritonavir increases methylergonovine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 24. Naloxegol: Ritonavir increases naloxegol levels, potentially precipitating opioid withdrawal symptoms. Co-administration is contraindicated. 25. Pimozide: Ritonavir increases pimozide levels, increasing the risk of QT interval prolongation. Co-administration is contraindicated. 26. Regorafenib: Ritonavir increases regorafenib levels while decreasing exposure to its active metabolites. Co-administration is contraindicated. 27. Salmeterol: Ritonavir increases salmeterol levels, leading to potential toxicity. Co-administration is contraindicated. 28. Simvastatin: Ritonavir increases simvastatin levels, leading to a higher risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Co-administration is contraindicated. 29. St. John’s Wort: St. John’s Wort decreases ritonavir levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 30. Tinidazole: Tinidazole increases ritonavir toxicity by inhibiting aldehyde dehydrogenase. This interaction is specific to ritonavir oral solution. Co-administration is contraindicated. 31. Venetoclax: Ritonavir increases venetoclax levels. Co-administration is contraindicated during the initial ramp-up phase. 32. Voclosporin: Ritonavir increases voclosporin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 33. Voriconazole: Ritonavir decreases voriconazole levels by increasing its metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 34. Acalabrutinib: Ritonavir increases acalabrutinib levels. Avoid co-administration with strong CYP3A inhibitors. 35. Adagrasib: Ritonavir increases adagrasib levels. Avoid co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. 36. Ado-trastuzumab emtansine: Ritonavir increases levels of the cytotoxic component DM1. Avoid co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. 37. Afatinib: Ritonavir increases afatinib levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Dose adjustment may be required. 38. Apalutamide: Apalutamide decreases ritonavir levels. Avoid co-administration. 39. Apixaban: Ritonavir increases apixaban levels. Avoid co-administration with strong dual inhibitors of CYP3A4 and P-gp. 40. Aprepitant: Ritonavir increases aprepitant levels. Avoid co-administration. 41. Atidarsagene autotemcel: Antiretroviral medications, including ritonavir, may interfere with cell manufacturing. Avoid ARTs for at least one month before cell mobilization. 42. Atorvastatin: Ritonavir increases atorvastatin toxicity. Avoid co-administration. 43. Avanafil: Ritonavir increases avanafil levels, leading to severe adverse events. Co-administration is contraindicated. 44. Avapritinib: Ritonavir increases avapritinib levels. Avoid co-administration. 45. Avatrombopag: Ritonavir increases avatrombopag levels. Avoid co-administration. 46. Axitinib: Ritonavir increases axitinib levels. Dose reduction may be required if co-administration is unavoidable. 47. Bedaquiline: Ritonavir increases bedaquiline levels. Avoid co-administration for more than 14 consecutive days unless benefits outweigh risks. 48. Betibeglogene autotemcel: Antiretroviral medications may interfere with cell manufacturing. Avoid ARTs for at least one month before mobilization. 49. Bosentan: Bosentan decreases ritonavir levels. Avoid co-administration. 50. Bosutinib: Ritonavir increases bosutinib levels. Avoid co-administration. 51. Brigatinib: Ritonavir increases brigatinib levels. Dose adjustment may be required if co-administration is unavoidable. 52. Bromocriptine: Ritonavir increases bromocriptine levels. Avoid co-administration. 53. Cabergoline: Ritonavir increases cabergoline levels. Co-administration is contraindicated. 54. Cabozantinib: Ritonavir increases cabozantinib levels. Dose adjustment may be required if co-administration is unavoidable. These interactions highlight the importance of careful consideration when prescribing ritonavir, particularly in combination with other medications metabolized by CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein.
